extracted.intended_audience: scientists, philosophers, and educated readers interested in the theory of organic evolution (late 19th-century readership)
extracted.subtask_description: A scholarly essay assessing competing explanations for organic evolution (natural selection, use/disuse inheritance, supernatural mind hypotheses), listing what classes of facts a satisfactory theory must explain and where particular hypotheses succeed or fail. Focuses on explanatory adequacy across multiple biological phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coherence of 'originating Mind' hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposition that an "originating Mind" is the cause of Evolution must be so conceived that its two terms can be united in thought; otherwise it can only be accepted as a matter of faith and not as an understanding-making statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: one cannot think of a single series of states of consciousness as antecedent to the infinity of simultaneous physical processes (motions of stars, planetary revolutions, countless terrestrial changes); attempting to ascribe such antecedence either divests Mind of its distinguishing attributes or forces an incoherent multiplication (plurality) of minds akin to fetishism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve distinguishing attributes in conceptual definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: If a hypothesized cause (e.g., Mind) is conceived 'under the guise of simple Dynamics', it must not be divested of the attributes by which it is distinguished, otherwise the conception (the word Mind) becomes a blank.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warning against diluting a term so it no longer retains the properties necessary for the concept to be meaningful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid conflating methodological naturalism with materialism
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine of Evolution in its purely scientific form does not necessarily involve Materialism; to represent it as doing so is a misunderstanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes scientific explanation in terms of matter and motion from metaphysical assertions that nothing remains to be explained; emphasizes that many proponents reject materialistic interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain complex adjustments/adaptations
rubrics_metrics.description: A satisfactory theory must make comprehensible remarkable adjusted structures (e.g., the pitcher-plant, Venus's fly-trap, the bladder-nosed seal's inflatable bag) that cannot reasonably be accounted for by direct effects of use or disuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin's hypothesis: successive selection of favourable variations can feasibly produce these complex appliances; use/disuse explanations are inadequate for such cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for the origin of new parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Theory must explain how entirely new parts or additions (e.g., duplicate sets of horns, increased numbers of vertebrae, additional mammary glands) can arise in lineages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spontaneous (fortuitous) variation plus establishment by inheritance/selection offers an explanation; direct functional causes (use/disuse) cannot account for sudden appearances or numeric changes in parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain changes in connexions/arrangements of parts
rubrics_metrics.description: A satisfactory theory must account for alterations in the relations or attachments of parts (e.g., changes in tendons' relations to bones), not merely changes in the bulk or size of components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Natural selection acting on favourable variations can establish novel modes of connexion that cannot be explained by simple functional augmentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain mimicry, resemblance, and deceptive coloration
rubrics_metrics.description: Theory must account for mimicry phenomena (leaf-insects, beetles resembling dew-drops, caterpillars like twigs, Batesian mimicry) and how such precise simulations arise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanism: an original slight resemblance leading to occasional survival advantages can be amplified generation after generation by natural selection until likeness becomes great; Darwin and Batesian explanations given as model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural selection is necessary but not necessarily sufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: While natural selection of favourable variations explains many phenomena, it by no means explains all that must be explained in organic evolution; other co-operating causes must be recognized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author contends that selection explains four chief classes of facts but that factors such as inheritance of functionally-produced modifications (Lamarckian effects) must be acknowledged as co-operators for a significant though smaller body of facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize cases inadequately explained by use/disuse
rubrics_metrics.description: A theory must recognize that many traits (thorns, seed coatings, delicate seed plumes, feather specialities, colors and patterns, deer horns' structure during growth) cannot plausibly result from direct effects of use or disuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides examples showing the physical impossibility or implausibility of direct functional causes producing these traits (e.g., deer horns are nerveless during growth; many plant hairs are never touched).

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for reductions owing to diminished use
rubrics_metrics.description: Some reductions in structure (e.g., decreased jaw size in civilized humans and indoor/lap dogs) are best explained by continued inheritance of diminutions consequent on diminished use rather than by natural selection, artificial selection, sexual selection, economy of nutrition, or simple correlation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author examines alternatives and rejects them (no selective advantage, artificial selection unlikely for internal muscle attachments, nutrition argument fails) and cites osteological evidence from skulls to support inheritance of reduced use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain coordinated changes of many cooperating parts
rubrics_metrics.description: A satisfactory theory must explain how complex useful actions involving many different parts, which must cooperate, can be brought about when constituent parts do not necessarily vary together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While coordinated enlargement of an entire limb can be understood if supply channels increase, there is proof that co-operative parts often do not vary synchronously; the theory must explain how beneficial multi-part coordination can evolve (author points to limitations and the need for mechanisms that can produce correlated variation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject empty verbal/teleological 'impulse' explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Explanations invoking an undefined 'impulse' (e.g., the Vestiges' supernatural impulse to advance) or similar verbal devices provide no real explanatory power and should be treated as inadequate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: such verbal solutions are compared to invoking 'Nature's abhorrence of a vacuum' — they do not aid understanding of the underlying facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical adequacy and critical tenability
rubrics_metrics.description: A theory must be tenable under critical examination and must be consistent with the full range of observed facts, not monopolized by those congruous with a prepossessed view while ignoring conspicuous incongruous facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author emphasizes the historical lack of tenable theories before Darwin and the importance of integrating wide-ranging observations rather than selectively attending to supporting evidence.
